item.title: How to Thrive Amid Uncertainty in an Endlessly Changing World
item.description:
Anxiety

How to Thrive Amid Uncertainty in an Endlessly Changing World

Turn the unknown from anxiety-inducing into a source of possibility.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • Not all uncertainty is the same. Five sources exist—and knowing them changes what you should do.
  • Uncertainty contains possibilities your brain may be filtering out.
  • Your brain can make uncertainty worse. Learning to shift its state can change what you see and do.
Source: Jorm Sangsorn/iStockphoto

People who have taken risks successfully will tell you that change is inevitable and that you should embrace it. Those who have survived the abyss of uncertainty will tell you to have strong faith and believe you will make it to the other side. Yet when you are trembling and unsure of your path, these recommendations are as reassuring as weather reports, leaving you staring blankly into the abyss of uncertainty that stands before you. What should you do when you feel uncertain in every waking moment, and how can you better manage yourself now, when the future seems bleak and impossible to navigate?

Neuroscience research has identified five key areas you can adjust to help navigate uncertainty.1 Uncertainty arises from ambiguous inputs, external and internal noise, insufficient information, or imperfect information processing. By addressing each of these factors progressively, you can become someone who thrives in uncertainty. When uncertainty hits, don’t try to solve everything. First ask: Where is the uncertainty coming from? Then use the three tools for your main source of uncertainty.

Ambiguous inputs: REINTERPRET

People may delay in responding to your e-mails, give you mixed signals about the safety of your job, or make you question your relationships. This ambiguity can be threatening. Neuroscience research indicates that some people are more prone to a negativity bias, though addressing this bias can help. There are three things that you can do:2

  • Question your first reaction. When something is ambiguous, your first interpretation may be more negative than the situation warrants.
  • Pause before deciding what it means. Give your brain time to consider other explanations.
  • Look for a more positive possibility. Ask yourself, “What else could this mean?”

External noise: FILTER

Every day, you’ll read something about the exponential rise of AI, threats to your job, random violent events, or some global catastrophe. It’s important to stay informed, but it’s also important to make a distinction between being informed vs. constantly forewarned. There are three things you can do.

  • Reduce the noise: Remove unnecessary distractions when possible.
  • Strengthen the signal: Make what matters stand out.3
  • Focus on the signal: Direct attention toward relevant information.

Internal noise: SETTLE

Sometimes, you are already perturbed, worried, overwhelmed, sad, or disappointed. This internal noise can make uncertainty feel worse. In fact, in 75% of cases, people under conditions of uncertainty mispredict that bad things will happen when they do not.4,5 There are three things that you can do.

  • Manage the internal noise: Do one thing to lighten the overwhelm that you are feeling
  • Use self-talk: Remind yourself that your brain is a natural negative exaggerator
  • Implement positive anticipation: Build one positive event into your day each week and look forward to it

Insufficient information: NAVIGATE

Sometimes the future is simply too unpredictable to know what will happen. You may have no idea whether your job will remain or not, or you may have no idea if you will find a relationship that you want or not. There are three things to consider here, too.

  • Switch from probability thinking to possibility thinking: Stop trying to predict things in unpredictable environments. Instead, visualize what you want and keep that in mind.6
  • Use existential confidence: Let your commitments determine your reality rather than the other way around.
  • Switch from control to observe: Rather than trying to uncontrol your life in an uncontrollable world, use your inner resources to observe and respond instead.

Imperfect processing: RESET

You may not be thinking about your future in the best way possible, or you may be limited in your resources to do any of the above. The first step is to accept that, rather than worry about it. Acceptance may help the brain become less caught up in the pain, reducing the strength with which brain systems involved in attention, emotion, and self-focused thinking converge on it.7 Here, too, there are three things that you can do.

  • Question your prior assumptions: Often, we come to any decision-making with expectations already baked into the brain, and then try to validate what we already believe.8 Question these expectations. e.g., that you will not find what you want
  • Imagine the opposite: For brief periods of time, use self-talk to tell yourself the exact opposite of your greatest worry.9
  • Self-compassion interrupts the inner critic: Notice the criticism, respond with kindness and understanding rather than attacking yourself, and remind yourself that struggle and imperfection are part of being human.10

You don't need to use all of these strategies at once. When uncertainty strikes, identify its main source: Is the situation ambiguous? Is there too much noise outside you or inside you? Do you simply not have enough information? Or might your own thinking need adjusting? Identify the source, then choose one of the three strategies that fits. The goal isn't to eliminate uncertainty. It's to become better at knowing what to do when it arrives.

item.title: Toxic Positivity Must Die
item.description:
Toxic Positivity

Toxic Positivity Must Die

Curiosity and acceptance are the answers to toxic positivity.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • Toxic positivity suppresses emotions.
  • True wellness requires acceptance, honesty, and empathy.
  • Remember that emotions are impermanent.
Source: Joanne Glaudemans / Unsplash

When someone tells you they’re sad, how do you respond? Do you tell them to look on the bright side? That things will get better? That it’s not that bad?

You may have fallen victim to the 21st-century blight of toxic positivity, the idea that “good vibes” cure all.

Scan any bookstore shelf, and you’ll see the evidence of toxic positivity and how far it’s invaded our lives. If fulfillment and contentment were as easy as making our bed or washing our face, we wouldn’t still be in our current mental health crisis.

Toxic Positivity

Toxic positivity is the idea that positivity begets positivity, that by acting happy, we somehow become happier. It’s the false assumption that we can reverse-engineer our own life satisfaction from the outside in.

Problem With Toxic Positivity

The problem with toxic positivity is that it leads to emotional suppression. It’s the modern-day version of walking it off, instead of feeling our feelings. When we’re told to smile or look on the bright side, we’re not given the time, space, or permission to feel our actual feelings and work through them in healthy and productive ways.

Solution to Toxic Positivity

The solution to toxic positivity is threefold: emotional acceptance, emotional honesty, and radical empathy.

Emotional Acceptance

Emotional acceptance is when you acknowledge how you’re feeling. It’s the opposite of emotional suppression. Some people get confused and think acceptance means liking or supporting your negative feelings, but it doesn’t. If I’m frustrated, emotional acceptance is owning that I’m frustrated. Acceptance can then allow me to ask for help or take a break. In contrast, suppression might lead to me bottling it up, taking it out on other people, or even blowing my top.

In a world of toxic positivity, we’re not supposed to be frustrated or have any other negative emotions, which means we’re pushing our feelings down. This leads to all kinds of negative physical and mental consequences.

Emotional Honesty

Emotional honesty is when we own up to our feelings to others. That means using our words and actually telling people how we’re doing. When someone asks you how you are, respond honestly.

Because of toxic positivity, we often tell people we’re good when we’re not. Let’s fight toxic positivity by telling people how we really are.

Radical Empathy

Finally, radical empathy means we let people feel what they’re feeling, instead of trying to force them to be OK. Sometimes, we’re not OK. When we get divorced or lose a loved one, we’re allowed to be sad or mad or any number of other so-called negative feelings. In fact, we’re allowed to have all the feelings all the time. Our feelings give us essential information for how to navigate through life. But we’re not privy to that information if we’re always lying about being happy and forcing others to do the same.

If someone says they’re cranky, ask them why or give them space. If someone is angry, don’t be defensive. Get curious. Curiosity is the antidote to shutting down other people’s feelings. Other people’s emotions can make us wildly uncomfortable. Fight that discomfort by getting curious about their anger, rage, discomfort, anxiety, overwhelm, upset, grief, or sadness.

Emotions Are Impermanent

Emotions are impermanent. Accepting them, being honest about them to others, and letting people experience them in their own time and in their own way helps emotions come and go. When we get stuck trying to be OK or good or even great, we’re not solving our mental health crisis. We’re not making ourselves happier. We’re not actually creating positivity. What we’re doing is suppressing our actual emotions, which allows them to linger and harm ourselves and our connection to others.

item.title: Dealing With a Bully? What the Science Says to Do
item.description:
Bullying

Dealing With a Bully? What the Science Says to Do

Informal supports are the best way to maintain self-worth when bullied.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • Bullies use their bullying to maintain popularity, hiding their emotional vulnerability.
  • The most effective anti-bullying interventions tend to favor informal solutions over formal programs.
  • Finding people who affirm our self-worth may be more effective than having others defend us directly.

With a new school year starting, and some not-so-good role models for our children in the news, it may be time to recall what research tells us about how to deal with a bully. In a recent well-cited review of the effectiveness of anti-bullying programs and recommendations for solutions, Christina Salmivalli and her colleagues at the University of Turku in Finland found that we may be overselling efforts to address bullying through formal interventions. First, though, a little about bullies and bullying.

Narcissism and Attention-Seeking

Bullies need to feed their narcissism. They cannot stand it when someone tells them they are wrong. Or weak. Or flawed. They must always perceive themselves as smarter and more important than everyone else. They have, however, one flaw: Their need for attention means they need victims.

That said, not all victims are equally vulnerable. According to Salmivalli, the age of the bullied child matters, with younger children more likely to be influenced positively by programs that influence the culture of a school or community and make bullying socially unacceptable. Unfortunately, older children, especially those between the ages of 13 and 15, respond far less well to such programs.

Helping a Child Cope With a Bully

Likewise, it can be difficult to say with certainty the best way to help a child cope with a bully. Strategies that hold the most hope include letting parents know what’s happening and encouraging them to support their child. Encouraging informal discussions among kids themselves is also a good idea. These informal approaches tend to report better outcomes in comparison to targeted interventions that teach children not to bully, or efforts to get bystanders to step in and help. Instead, less formal strategies may be easier for children to accept. When those who are bullied and those watching the bullying name the behavior for what it is (a narcissist trying to elevate their status), and lots of people condemn what the bully is doing, then it is more likely the bully becomes the one who is weakened rather than their victims.

Once there is agreement that the bully is acting badly, the bully is effectively undermined, labelled for what they are: a social misfit doing harm to others. Meanwhile, those who are bullied are provided with the empathy they need to maintain a sense of well-being. It seems that a little support from many different people goes a long way to giving back to those who are bullied their self-respect.

Status also plays a role in these patterns of interaction between bullies and those they bully. Bullies tend to be people who are perceived as popular but not necessarily liked. Their attacks on those with lesser status are an easy win for them, but increasingly, research is suggesting that bullies also attack higher-status peers because it brings the bully even more power.

article continues after advertisement

So, what else works besides informal networks of people who create a culture that labels the act of bullying as distasteful and a sign of weakness? Capitulation does not work. Giving in to endless erratic and senseless demands by a bully only makes bullies feel and act with impunity. Negotiating with a bully is senseless, too, as they don’t want to share power: They want the status that comes from power over others. No wonder that paying a bully to be left alone (e.g., giving in to extortion) is not a great strategy that works long-term either. The bully will just keep pushing, and pushing, and pushing for more power (and the child’s lunch money) because power is what protects a bully’s fragile sense of self-esteem.

Likewise, having others defend the victim may work, but the best strategy is to simply secure allies. Not formal defenders, but those who become friends and stand with the child who is bullied. Think of this as not so much a direct attack on the actions of the bully but an affirmation that those who are bullied are better than the bully. To exist in a community of people who empathize with what a bullied child is experiencing increases the bullied child’s status. It is an inoculation against feelings of self-loathing. It encourages the victim of bullying to ignore the darn bully, turn their back on them, and seek out places where a bullied child can feel whole and appreciated, preventing those who are bullied from feeling isolated and weak.

Even better, laugh at the bully, behind their back if one must. Bullies, after all, hate to be seen as small or ignored. It reminds them how silly they look and how little power they actually have in the eyes of their peers.

It’s not easy to use these strategies when the bullying is incessant. If the science is solid, however, then what we know is that those who are bullied may experience the resilience to live through the bullying and grow to be much stronger, happier, and better connected by relying on their informal networks of like-minded peers and adults. And those are the last things the bully wants their victims to experience, if only because those are the very things the bully craves but fails to achieve.
